extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying restriction/election rules (including nucleotide-sequence-specific waivers) and for identifying and making statutory and nonstatutory double patenting rejections during patent prosecution and reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election and fee requirement or petition under 37 CFR 1.129(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must either: (1) elect the invention or inventions to be searched and examined and pay the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(s) for each independent and distinct invention in excess of one which applicant elects; or (2) file a petition under 37 CFR 1.129(b) traversing the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this form paragraph in all restriction or election of species requirements made in applications subject to the transition restriction provisions set forth in 37 CFR 1.129(b). Procedure NOT applicable to any design or reissue application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refund when divided inventions rejoined because linking claim allowable (transitional applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever divided inventions in a transitional application are rejoined because a linking claim is allowable and applicant paid the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(s) for the additional invention, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 809, § 821.04, and § 821.04(a). Applies where linking claim allows rejoinder; examiner should notify applicant of refund possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refund when additional species embraced by allowable generic claim (transitional applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever claims drawn to an additional species in a transitional application for which applicant paid the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(s) are no longer withdrawn from consideration because they are fully embraced by an allowable generic claim, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The determination of when claims to nonelected species would no longer be withdrawn from consideration should be made as indicated in MPEP § 806.04(d), § 821.04, and § 821.04(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nucleotide sequences normally independent and distinct inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Polynucleotide molecules defined by their nucleic acid sequence that encode different proteins are structurally distinct chemical compounds and are thus deemed to normally constitute independent and distinct inventions within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 121 and 37 CFR 1.141 et seq.; absent evidence to the contrary, each such nucleotide sequence is presumed to represent an independent and distinct invention, subject to a restriction requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To aid biotechnology industry, Director partially waived 37 CFR 1.141 et seq. to permit a reasonable number of such nucleotide sequences to be claimed in a single application (Examination of Patent Applications Containing Nucleotide Sequences, 1192 O.G. 68 (Nov. 19, 1996)). See MPEP § 1850 for international/PCT treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: General numerical waiver for nucleotide sequences (ten-sequence guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been determined that normally ten sequences constitute a reasonable number for examination purposes. Accordingly, in most cases, up to ten independent and distinct nucleotide sequences will be examined in a single application without restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to the specifically selected sequences, those sequences which are patentably indistinct from the selected sequences will also be examined. Nucleotide sequences encoding the same protein are not considered independent and distinct and will be examined together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional cases and petition for additional nucleotide sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In some exceptional cases, the complex nature of the claimed material may necessitate that the reasonable number of sequences to be selected be less than ten. Applicants may petition pursuant to 37 CFR 1.181 for examination of additional nucleotide sequences by providing evidence that the different nucleotide sequences do not cover independent and distinct inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 37 CFR 1.181 petitions and provide supporting evidence demonstrating lack of independence/distinctness among sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of alternative individual-sequence claims (example A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications claiming more than ten individual independent and distinct nucleotide sequences in alternative form (e.g., an isolated DNA fragment comprising DNA having at least 95% identity to a DNA sequence selected from SEQ ID Nos. 1-1,000) will be subject to a restriction requirement; only the ten nucleotide sequences selected in response to the restriction requirement and any other claimed sequences which are patentably indistinct therefrom will be examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant claims >10 alternative individual sequences, require election to ten and examine selected plus patentably indistinct sequences only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of combination claims of nucleotide sequences (example B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications claiming only a combination of nucleotide sequences (e.g., comprising SEQ ID Nos. 1-1,000) will generally not be subject to a restriction requirement. The presence of one novel and nonobvious sequence within the combination will render the entire combination allowable. The combination will be searched until one nucleotide sequence is found to be allowable; if no individual sequence is allowable, examiner will consider whether the combination as a whole renders the claim allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner chooses order of searching to maximize identification of an allowable sequence. If an allowable sequence is found, all combinations containing that sequence will be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of composition claims reciting different combinations (example C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications containing composition claims reciting different combinations of individual nucleotide sequences (e.g., a combination containing at least thirty different DNA fragments selected from SEQ ID Nos. 1-1,000) will be subject to a restriction requirement. Applicants must select one combination for examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If selected combination contains ≤10 sequences, all sequences of the combination will be searched. If >10 sequences, examine following the procedure for combination claims (example B): search until one sequence is allowable; identification of any allowable sequences causes all combinations containing allowed sequences to be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling applications with mixed claim types (examples A–C)
rubrics_metrics.description: In applications containing claims of the types in examples (A)-(C), the Office will require restriction of the application to ten sequences for initial examination purposes. Based upon the finding of allowable sequences, claims limited to individual sequences and combinations containing the allowable sequences and any patentably indistinct sequences will be rejoined and allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonelected claims requiring any allowable nucleotide sequence(s) should be considered for rejoinder. Follow MPEP § 821.04 for rejoinder procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine and public policy of double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of double patenting seeks to prevent the unjustified extension of patent exclusivity beyond the term of a patent. Double patenting results when the right to exclude granted by a first patent is unjustly extended by the grant of a later issued patent or patents; the focus of any double patenting analysis is on the claims in the multiple patents or patent applications involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double patenting analysis considers common inventorship/ownership/joint research agreements (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) and (3)). See cited case law (e.g., In re Zickendraht; In re Van Ornum) and MPEP § 804.03 for ownership treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations where double patenting issues can be raised
rubrics_metrics.description: A double patenting issue may arise between two or more pending applications, or between one or more pending applications and a patent. It may also arise in reexamination proceedings between the patent claims being reexamined and the claims of one or more applications and/or patents; double patenting does not relate to international applications which have not yet entered the U.S. national stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional double patenting rejections can be made where appropriate without waiting for the first patent to issue, provided confidential status of applications (35 U.S.C. 122) is not violated. See subsection discussions for treatment in reexamination (MPEP § 2258).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconditions for double patenting analysis (ownership/common inventorship/joint research agreements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before consideration can be given to double patenting, two or more patents or applications must have at least one common inventor and/or be either commonly assigned/owned or non-commonly assigned/owned but subject to a joint research agreement as set forth in 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) and (3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments to 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (CREATE Act) require treating certain non-commonly owned subject matter as if commonly owned for double patenting purposes; see MPEP § 804.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two types of double patenting rejections (statutory vs nonstatutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are generally two types of double patenting rejections: (1) the 'same invention' statutory-type double patenting rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 101, and (2) the 'nonstatutory-type' double patenting rejection (obviousness-type) based on judicial doctrine to prevent prolongation of patent term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonstatutory double patenting may include one-way or two-way obviousness determinations. Rare factual circumstances may give rise to other nonstatutory forms; use appropriate form paragraphs (8.33–8.39) for nonstatutory rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinations required before making a double patenting rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether a proper basis exists to enter a double patenting rejection, the examiner must determine: (A) whether a double patenting rejection is prohibited by the third sentence of 35 U.S.C. 121; (B) whether a statutory basis exists; and (C) whether a nonstatutory basis exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each determination must be made on the basis of all facts in the application before the examiner. Charts I-A, I-B, II-A, and II-B illustrate methodology. Domination is distinct from double patenting and by itself cannot support a double patenting rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory double patenting test (same invention / literal infringement test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reliable test for double patenting under 35 U.S.C. 101 is whether a claim in the application could be literally infringed without literally infringing a corresponding claim in the patent. If an embodiment falls within the scope of one claim but not the other, identical subject matter is not defined by both claims and statutory double patenting does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is determined that the same invention is being claimed twice, 35 U.S.C. 101 precludes the grant of the second patent regardless of the presence or absence of a terminal disclaimer. Examples: 'halogen' vs 'chlorine' and '36 inches' vs '3 feet' illustrate scope considerations. Use form paragraphs 8.30–8.32 as headings/paragraphs for statutory rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer cannot overcome statutory double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: A filing of a terminal disclaimer cannot overcome a double patenting rejection based upon 35 U.S.C. 101 (statutory 'same invention' type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 8.30 must be used as a heading for all subsequent statutory double patenting rejections; follow form paragraphs 8.31 or 8.32 for the substantive rejection and examiner notes for applicable situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for provisional ODP rejections between copending applications (terminal disclaimer rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'provisional' obviousness-type double patenting (ODP) rejection may be made between copending applications. If a provisional ODP rejection is the only rejection remaining in the earlier-filed application while the later-filed application is rejectable on other grounds, the examiner should withdraw that rejection and permit the earlier-filed application to issue without a terminal disclaimer. If the ODP rejection is the only rejection remaining in the later-filed application while the earlier-filed application is rejectable on other grounds, a terminal disclaimer must be required in the later-filed application before the rejection can be withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ODP rejections exist in two applications where both are otherwise free of other rejections, withdraw ODP in the earlier-filed app to allow it to issue; require terminal disclaimer in later-filed before withdrawal. If applications filed same day, determine base vs improvement claims; base application's ODP can be withdrawn without a terminal disclaimer; improvement application cannot. For three conflicting applications, terminal disclaimers must be filed in at least two to link all three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting analysis parallels 35 U.S.C. 103 Graham factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting rejection is appropriate where conflicting claims are not identical but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined claim is anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s). The analysis parallels the guidelines for analysis of a 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Graham factual inquiries: (A) determine scope and content of the patent claim relative to the application claim; (B) determine differences between them; (C) determine level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (D) evaluate any objective indicia of nonobviousness. The patent principally underlying the double patenting rejection is not considered prior art in this analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting considerations in reexamination proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A double patenting issue may raise a substantial new question of patentability of a claim of a patent and thus be addressed in a reexamination proceeding. Double patenting may exist where a reference patent or application and the patent under reexamination are filed by inventive entities with at least one common inventor and/or a common owner/assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent under reexamination was granted on or after December 10, 2004, double patenting may also exist where the inventions resulted from activities under a joint research agreement pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) and (3), provided evidence of the joint research agreement has been made of record. A double patenting rejection may NOT be made on the basis of statutory double patenting if the patent under reexamination issued before December 10, 2004. The prior art exclusion under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) cannot be used to overcome an obvious double patenting rejection.
